1.pericope_label: The consecration: its shape and its principle

schools.summary: Gill states the object in a word, to hallow and set apart; Calvin declines a full treatment here, promising it at Leviticus, disclaims inventing mysteries out of vague speculations, and compresses his reading into one line — because every man's uncleanness bars his access to God, the priests are washed first, from which he gathers that the purity only typified under the law is found in Christ alone.

Henry reads the solemnity as aimed at priests and people alike, works the Hebrew idiom of filling the hand into two things about ministers — their hands are full, and their hands must be filled from above — and finds the door of the tent a fitting place for men who were to be doorkeepers.
Clarke gives the sequence as a table of contents and enters the chronological caution that the consecration did not take place until after the tabernacle was erected.
Ellicott sets out the rite as five acts — ablution, investiture, anointing, sacrifice, filling of the hand — each symbolical, so that the whole forms an acted parable.

themes: a promise to say more later

2.pericope_label: The bread, the flour and the basket

schools.summary: Gill records the wheaten flour and the single basket in which everything was carried.
Clarke counts three kinds of bread and distinguishes them by their Hebrew names and forms — the general unleavened, the pricked or perforated cake, and the wafer from a root meaning to be made thin.

Ellicott explains the requirement of unleavened bread as purity, fermentation being viewed as a species of corruption, renders 'without blemish' more strictly as perfect, and distinguishes a thick cake with oil poured over it from a biscuit extremely thin and unsubstantial; Keil and Delitzsch list the same three with the material and the carriage.
Gill reads the girding for its moral, Aaron with the girdle of the ephod and his sons with common girdles, all showing what strength, diligence and expedition the office required.

Clarke derives 'invest' from the vesting itself, and makes anointing the mark of the Spirit's gifts at the installing of prophets, priests and kings — from which he argues that since no man held all three offices, none but Jesus ever bore the title of the Anointed One. Wesley gives each act its meaning as it comes: washed because they must be clean, clothed because the graces of the Spirit must be put on, girded as men strengthened for work, robed and crowned as men who counted their office their honour.

Ellicott treats this as the first religious ablution in Scripture, canvasses its parallels in Egypt, Persia, Greece and Italy, and answers the objection they raise — Sinai was not meant to annul natural religion but to improve it; he counts nine distinct acts in the investiture and thinks directions this minute justify the equally minute ones of the English Ordinal.

10.pericope_label: The bullock for a sin offering

schools.summary: Gill identifies the parts burnt and reads the burning outside the camp as representing a whole Christ under all his sufferings and the shame he underwent in them.

Clarke describes the laying on of hands as consecrating the animal and transferring the offerer's forfeited life to it, and records the later form of confession spoken over the victim; Wesley grounds the whole offering in the priests' own infirmity — they must offer for their own sin first — and reads the burning outside the camp as signifying the imperfection of the legal dispensation, since a better high priest had to be looked for.

Ellicott states the transfer starkly: the offerer identified himself with the animal, the animal became accursed, its death paid the penalty and the guilty went free, as Christ was made a curse for us; he gives the fixed rule for blood on the horns and at the base, explains why fat was thought fitting for the altar, and notes that a sin offering was reckoned too impure for any part to be human food.

15.pericope_label: The ram for a burnt offering

schools.summary: Calvin, treating the consecration as a whole, states the principle that the priest must be sprinkled with blood in order to conciliate God's favour for the purpose of intercession, and answers the objection that only the right members were smeared by holding that in the one part the other is comprehended; he reads the ear for obedience and the hands and feet for the whole course of a life, and denies that the tongue is in view since intercession, not teaching, is the office concerned. Gill notes the parts laid in order because the whole was to be burnt.

Wesley fixes the order — sin offering first, since until guilt is removed no acceptable service can be performed — and reads the ram wholly burnt as the men's dedication of themselves, living sacrifices ascending in the flame of holy love; Clarke marks it simply as a burnt offering.

Ellicott explains why the whole might be consumed here where only parts of a sin offering could be, corrects 'sprinkle' to 'scatter' and describes the casting of blood on two corners so as to wet all four sides, and refuses to let 'a sweet savour' be read as the heathen notion that gods are pleased by odour.

19.pericope_label: The ram of consecration, and blood on ear, thumb and toe

schools.summary: Gill is careful about the mechanics, the blood taken being what stood in the basin rather than what had been thrown against the altar.

Clarke explains the name as the ram of filling up, carries the custom sideways into the Eastern present brought to a superior and into the Bible placed in an English priest's hands at ordination, and reads the three members as dedicating all their faculties while teaching that none of them could hear, work or walk acceptably without the blood; Wesley makes it a peace offering in which they had the comfort of the priesthood, the blood divided between God and them as a mutual covenant, and the extremities marked so that the whole man was taken in.

Ellicott calls this by far the most peculiar part of the ceremony and the act that actually imparted the priestly character; he begins from blood as the life, given back by God to consecrate his ministers, and reads the twofold sprinkling of blood and oil as justification and sanctification together.
Gill takes the filled hands forward to the antitype, all things relative to God's glory and his people's good being in Christ's hands, so that he too has somewhat to offer.

Clarke supplies Ludolf's account of the fat-tailed sheep and the little cart its owners tie behind it, treats Aaron and his sons at this point as still private persons offering through a priest, and relays Houbigant's conjecture — with an apology for its boldness — that the waving and heaving traced the figure of the cross; he notes with some relish that Moses, never consecrated himself, here acts as high priest and takes the priest's portion. Wesley describes the waving and burning as God admitting them to wait at his table.

Ellicott would read the offerings placed on their hands rather than in them, with Moses' hands beneath, so that Aaron and his sons performed their first priestly act as passive instruments moved by his muscular energy — which is what completed their priestly character.

themes: the fat tail and the cart
on the hands, not in them

26.pericope_label: The perpetual due, the succession, and the seven days

schools.summary: Gill grounds the two portions in the high priest's dress, the shoulder because he bore the tribes' names on his shoulders and the breast because he bore them on his heart, and records the Targum's insistence that the successor be of Aaron's own family; Calvin reads every restriction — strangers barred, place fixed, remainder burnt — as guarding one thing, that no corruption creep in to pollute the service or render it contemptible, and calls the whole a childish rudiment suited to that people's infirmity.

Clarke turns the seven days into an excursus on the number itself, from the Hebrew number of perfection through the Essene formula preserved by Philo and Josephus to the Pythagorean triangle and square, and ends by leaving the ancient philosophers to judge their own meaning. Wesley reads the eating as friendship, God supping with them and they with him.
Ellicott accounts for Moses receiving the breast by the general law of wave offerings, which assigned it to whoever officiated.

themes: seven as a number of perfection

35.pericope_label: Seven days, and the altar sanctified

schools.summary: Gill reads the sevenfold repetition as figuring the full expiation these offerings could not themselves obtain; Calvin faces the difficulty that an altar typifying Christ should need cleansing, and answers with his rule that no similitude is identical with the reality, the likeness holding where it matters — that God could be propitiated only by an expiation made with blood.

Wesley explains why a rite performed in one day took seven to complete, as putting a distance between the old state and the new and obliging the men to pause over the weight of the work; he reads the daily sin offering as teaching that atonement made does not end penitence, and that sacrifices repeated daily could not perfect the comers, so a better hope had to be looked for. Clarke reads the closing clause as property, whatever was laid on the altar becoming the Lord's.

Ellicott takes seven as the number used under the old covenant wherever acts reach their result by repetition, would render 'by' making atonement rather than 'when', and turns the last clause into a prohibition — nothing unholy must touch the altar, the future carrying the force of an imperative.

debates.question: What does "whatsoever toucheth the altar shall be holy" mean?

sides.position: the altar sanctifies the victims laid on it
whatever was laid on it became the Lord's property, devoted to sacred use
it is an imperative — nothing that is not holy may touch it

schools.summary: Calvin gives the daily sacrifice first place among all offerings, explains why a daily victim was needed alongside the yearly entry into the holiest, refuses to let the oil and wine be read as flavouring — God was not gratified by their savour, nor did he wish to make epicures of the priests under colour of religion — and takes 'continual' as temporary on Daniel's authority, ceasing at the coming of Christ. Gill marks the same terminus.
Henry notes that whatever else might be offered, these two were sure to be offered at the public charge, for the daily sins and the daily mercies of all Israel.

Clarke traces the ordinance from the settlement in Canaan to the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans; Wesley reads the two lambs as typifying Christ's continual intercession, so that one offering made once for all becomes continual, and draws the practical lesson of prayer morning and evening.
Keil and Delitzsch supply the measures and are candid about their uncertainty, Bertheau and Thenius differing by nearly half and the Rabbins reckoning by hen's eggs.

themes: oil and wine not for savour

schools.summary: Calvin settles the name of the tent by philology, the root meaning to contract or meet for mutual business, so that it is the place God appointed for himself and his people to come together; he presses that God alone sanctifies place, offerings and men, and turns that against those who claim more than God has conferred. Gill describes the dwelling in practice, God residing in the tent set in the middle of the camp like a king in his palace.

Clarke infers from the promise to sanctify that Moses' consecration was only symbolical and that no designation by man can qualify anyone for holy things, calls the indwelling the great charter of God's people under both Testaments, and reads 'know' as acknowledge.

Ellicott extends the sanctifying past the ceremony to God's continual presence with the priesthood in their ministerial acts and daily walk, and warns against reducing the indwelling to the presence of the cloud, since it pledged a perpetual supervision and protection the nation's history bears out.

themes: the tent of meeting, so named
more than a cloud in a tent
the end the whole rite served
